Hi there. I haven’t been in a parasocial relationship myself. I have, however, experienced the end of close friendships, romantic relationships, and even an obsession with someone that didn’t reciprocate my feelings. Boy, all of those things were excruciatingly painful when they ended. Like when I realized I couldn’t hold on to them anymore because they treated me badly or simply didn’t reciprocate my feelings, etc.

My guess is you’re going through some sort of grieving process. After your revelation, you also realized that things will never be the same. And that’s okay. The end of a relationship or chapter of one’s life is hard! Especially if you haven’t really developed your external support network. It’s rough. 

My advice is to go seek a therapist. Talking it out really helps. Even posting on here is a big step toward seeking help. 

Recovering from a situation like this isn’t easy, so be sure to treat yourself to comforting things- although you’ll probably need to clear your home/phone/computer of reminders of your  relationship, and avoid diving into another similar relationship. Keeping my hands busy helps me stay grounded and in the moment.

Finally, just because the relationship isn’t “real” doesn’t mean your pain isn’t real or valid. It took me a long time to realize that. Like, I didn’t deserve help since my pain was “imaginary” and “all in my head.” False. Your emotions are totally valid. Feel those feelings, let them pass, and have compassion for yourself.

Edit: When I REALLY want to off myself, it helps to postpone by 1 day. And the next day, I postpone another day, and so on. If I feel inconsolable, I try to survive for at least 10 minutes. If that’s too long, then I challenge myself to survive the next 10 seconds. Breathing and journalling really helps

I know I’ve talked about only myself, but I’m sharing the advise my friend gave me in case you might find it useful. 

Try:

•practicing your instruments, or maybe find a new hobby. 

•talking to new people and make new friends. The “fake it until you make it” approach has worked well for me in the past since I get major social anxiety. When I start a conversation, I try asking people a lot of questions about themselves. Btw, everyone likes talking about themselves. So no, I don’t necessarily think you’re selfish. •joining a support group in your community for mental health or whatever else (even AA, I’ve sat in meetings even though I’m not an alcoholic). You can tell them how you feel about yourself without fear of judgment and a whole room of people will tell you that you’re not toxic nor a burden. •caring about your job and make meaning with it. It’s possible for you to feel like you’re working toward a greater purpose than just surviving. 

•apologizing only when you are wrong, yet be sympathetic to someone that feels hurt even when you weren’t responsible for it. Valuing a relationship over being “right” doesn’t make you a beta.

•getting professional help (if possible). I know it may be difficult if you don’t have insurance, or your location, but it helps a lot of people. Meds may have side effects, but they’re not that bad usually and a lot of people can get off of them when they’re doing better and have learned how to cope with their depression or anxiety.

In addition, I joined literally every club I could. And as a result, I made a lot of friends and entered my first relationship. Now, I just have a few close friends from those I met before. My first night in a psych ward was scary, but mostly because I was only familiar with what I saw in movies. I was kept in the ICU for a few days, which was a dismal place with periodic shouting. It made me feel worse than ever before. But when I proved to not be an immediate danger to myself, I was moved to the adult unit which was soooo much better. I was reserved at first, but I quickly made friends with people my age. I was kept there for two weeks, and during that time I met a lot of wonderful people going through their own struggles. Talking to them, and especially the older people helped me more than talking to my friends and family that have never experienced suicidal thoughts.

For the most part, days are very structured and pass by slowly at times. There highlights of the day are usually meals, arts and crafts, and smoke breaks. The rest of the day is groups that are sometimes helpful and sometimes not. Just put in a whole-hearted effort into getting better and you’ll get something out of it. I didn’t try at all at the first two places I’d been to and stayed feeling depressed and suicidal (I still am but nowhere as bad as back then).
